title: DIRECT APPROACHES FOR THE MINIMAX PROBLEM
contribution: Synthesises the Charalambous-Conn nonlinear and Bartels-Conn-Charalambous linear minimax algorithms into one stable, projection-based direct method that works on M_f(x)=max f_i(x) itself, with horizontal/vertical directions, QR updating that exploits linear f_i, and a breakpoint line search.
problem_entry: Nonsmoothness of max_i f_i at ties blocks gradient methods; instead of solving the equivalent NLP P* (Waren-Lasdon-Suchman), use P* only to get a direction and move directly on M_f (pp. 1, 3).
key_idea: d = -Pe with P the projector onto the null space of active-constraint gradients in (z,x)-space; horizontal step keeps the eps-near-active set, vertical least-squares step levels it; drop by sign of w = R^{-1}Q1^T e (pp. 2-6).
assumptions: f_i in C^2; active gradients linearly independent, degeneracy handled by negligible perturbations; convergence under some fairly natural assumptions (paraphrase) proved elsewhere [5] (pp. 1, 7).
proof_devices: local Taylor argument that -Pe decreases all active functions in the linear/concave case (7)-(9) and in the convex case (10)-(11) (pp. 2-3)
restating the rival (Barrodale-Phillips dual) algorithm stage by stage in primal/projection terms (pp. 8-9)
experiments: none here; delegated to reports [3], [5] and to the microwave-network application paper [6] (p. 9)
positioning: Improves on [5] (stability, exploiting linearity); detailed comparison with Bartels-Conn-Charalambous [3], Cline [10] (Haar only), Barrodale-Phillips dual (no well-documented evidence of superiority) and Zangwill (drops vertical step, tolerance to zero) (pp. 7-9).
writing: Informal-first exposition with contour figures, then a numbered algorithm; ends the positioning with a rhetorical question on dual vs direct methods; frank about missing numbers and the non-obvious second-order extension (pp. 1, 9).
limits_future: No numbers or proofs in the paper; steepest-descent-like in subspaces; second-order generalisation 'not obvious, even assuming it is desirable'; constraints can be added naturally (p. 9).

problem_entry: External readers (A. Ben-Tal, J. Zowe) found an incorrectly stated second-order condition (p. 1).

title: Nonlinear programming via an exact penalty function: Global analysis
contribution: A second-order exact l1-penalty method for inequality-constrained NLP (projected Newton horizontal step, least-squares vertical step, multiplier-based dropping, breakpoint line search, mu reduction) with a global convergence proof, Gill-Murray-style implementation and preliminary numbers; the rate is in a twin report.
problem_entry: Conn-Pietrzykowski's first-order projected penalty method converges globally but only linearly; nondifferentiability of p(x,mu) is the obstacle (pp. 4-6).
key_idea: Minimise the second-order change in p subject to zero second-order change in eps-active constraints, approximated via a min-max Lagrangian with lagged multipliers: h=-Z(Z^T B Z)^{-1} Z^T grad p, plus v=-A(A^T A)^{-1}Phi and a dropping step when lambda_j not in [0,1/mu] (pp. 6-9).
assumptions: C^2; iterates in compact W; finitely many stationary points; first-order points strict second-order; linear independence of eps-active gradients; sufficient-decrease line search; consistent projected-Hessian approximation (pp. 17-18, 22).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: p(x+h+v)-p(x) <= -delta(||Z^T grad p||^2+||Phi||_1) near a strict second-order point, via separate Taylor expansions of the smooth part and the active constraints (pp. 18-22)
six-part global proof; contradiction p(x^k) -> -infinity from the sufficient-decrease condition rules out infinitely many drops (pp. 23-26)
finiteness of non-optimal stationary points gives a uniform descent constant (Part 3, p. 24)
experiments: 8 classic problems (Rosen-Suzuki, Wong, Powell, Colville 1-3, Chamberlain 1-2), 11 problem/start runs; best and worst penalty-function evaluation counts over a parameter box; accuracy digits (p. 26)
positioning: Upgrades Conn-Pietrzykowski [9] to second order; borrows Gill-Murray linearly-constrained techniques and Bartels-Conn-Sinclair perturbation for degeneracy; Murray-Overton cited for an alternative piecewise line search (pp. 6, 12, 15-16).
writing: Motivation section derives each direction from a 'minimise change subject to zero change' principle; admits the direction-choice rule is 'somewhat arbitrary' while stressing the theory covers 'any number of selection rules' (pp. 5-10).
limits_future: Scaling and parameter choice not addressed; mu-safeguards not guaranteed; future: full projected quasi-Newton implementation and scaling (pp. 13, 15, 27).

title: Generalizing the LINPACK condition estimator
contribution: Two O(n^2) generalisations of the LINPACK condition estimator for triangular factors, 'look-behind' (rotating the earlier right-hand side) and divide-and-conquer, in L2 and L1 versions, with an empirical reliability study.
problem_entry: Reliable condition estimation in O(n^2) after factorisation; LINPACK relies on an unproven greedy heuristic and has counterexamples (pp. 5-9, 21).
key_idea: Choose at each step a rotation (c,s) that rescales the previous d and sets the new component, maximising a quadratic (L2, closed form via phi'(a)=0) or convex (L1, endpoint check) growth measure; or combine subsystems recursively by the same rotation (pp. 11-16).
assumptions: A already factored, T lower triangular; fixed nonnegative weights; no reliability theorem (pp. 10-11).
proof_devices: SVD argument ||z||/||w|| >= ||A^{-1}|| cos(v_n,d) motivating a large-norm solution (p. 8)
closed-form 1-D maximisation over a rotation angle giving two sine-cosine candidates (pp. 12, 15)
convexity in lambda implies only endpoints lambda in {0,1} need checking (p. 13)
experiments: 1000 random and 1000 pivoted-QR triangular matrices (n=5..50) plus 250 L1 cases; binned distributions of true/estimated singular-value ratios for three variants (pp. 18-20)
positioning: Extends Cline-Moler-Stewart-Wilkinson (LINPACK); compares Forsythe-Moler and Karasalo; cites Cline's counterexamples to LINPACK (pp. 6-7, 21-22).
writing: Conclusion refuses to rank estimators on experiments, admits an easy counterexample to its own divide-and-conquer method, and names provable reliability as the goal (p. 21).
limits_future: No proofs; sigma_1 estimates consistently inferior with no explanation; future: a rigorous result for T from pivoted QR (pp. 19, 21).

title: On the location of directions of infinite descent for nonlinear programming algorithms
contribution: Characterises existence of solutions to equality-constrained QPs by inertia and shows how null-space, Lagrangian and range-space methods can extract directions of linear infinite descent or negative curvature from the generalised Cholesky factors they already compute, with operation counts and a small experiment.
problem_entry: EQP subproblems in SQP/active-set methods may have no finite solution; a direction of infinite descent then signals a bad estimate or active set and can repair both (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: One factorisation for existence and step: inertia identities In(K)=In(Z^T H Z)+(t,t,0) decide the case; dolids are projections of the rhs onto null spaces, doncs combinations of conjugate negative vectors read off the block-diagonal D (pp. 4-11).
assumptions: A full rank t <= n; n small enough for dense direct solves; H nonsingular for range-space methods (pp. 1, 4, 8, 12).
proof_devices: inertia identity In(K)=In(Z^T H Z)+(t,t,0) turning existence into counting (Lemma 1.2, p. 4)
Fredholm-type alternative: Nx=b solvable or exists y with Ny=0, b^T y=1 (Lemma 2.1, p. 6)
counting: k>t conjugate negative vectors admit a combination satisfying t homogeneous constraints (p. 8)
structural-zero argument that N is lower triangular-like, so elimination has no structural fill-in (p. 11)
experiments: pseudo-random EQPs, n=30, t=1..29, H diagonal with 6 negative eigenvalues, A full; measures columns processed, share of superdiagonals eliminated, multiplications; residuals ~1e-16 (pp. 14-16)
positioning: Null-space version basically Bunch-Kaufman 1980; Lagrangian and range-space extensions new; negative-curvature lineage Fletcher-Freeman, Sorensen, More-Sorensen, Goldfarb; relies on Gould 1983 (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Coins acronyms (dolid, donc); equivalence theorems with one-line proofs; explicitly hedged experiments ('by no means exhaustive') (pp. 2, 5, 14).
limits_future: Open: how triangular N is, how many range-space columns are needed; future: Ap=d, sparse variants trading stability for structure via threshold pivoting, factor updating (pp. 14, 17).

title: The computational structure and characterization of nonlinear discrete Chebyshev problems
contribution: Generalises linear Chebyshev concepts (reference, levelled reference) to nonlinear discrete Chebyshev and minimax problems via cadres and cadre multipliers, proves every local minimiser carries a levelled reference set, and shows the levelling (vertical) direction is a descent direction, enabling multiple dropping.
problem_entry: Existing nonlinear minimax methods lean on the underlying NLP; linear Chebyshev algorithms succeed by exploiting the solution's characterisation, while classical nonlinear theory is not computable for discrete problems (pp. 4-5, 10).
key_idea: Characterise-then-compute: locate a cadre, sign-correct it into a reference set, level it with v=-A(A^T A)^{-1}Phi, which decreases all active functions; negative cadre multipliers yield multiple dropping (pp. 12-31).
assumptions: f_i in C^1; local minima; stationary points nondegenerate for working-set equivalence; Lemma 37 exact only in the linear case (pp. 3, 18, 20, 25).
proof_devices: Gordan's theorem (Lemma 34, p. 22)
write grad f_mu as a convex combination of gradient differences via cadre multipliers so grad f_mu^T v = -sum lambda_j (f_mu - f_ij) < 0 (Lemma 35, pp. 22-23)
sign-flip construction (7.5) of a reference set from a non-reference cadre (p. 24)
normalised-multiplier identity (7.16) ordering decrease rates (Lemmas 39-40, pp. 28-30)
experiments: none; the algorithm is in companion report [10] (p. 32)
positioning: Contrasts NLP-based minimax methods (Murray-Overton, Womersley-Fletcher, Hald-Madsen, Han, Watson); builds on Descloux's cadre, Brannigan's minimum H-set, Rice's nonlinear theory, the Remez algorithm and the authors' linear l_inf work (pp. 4, 12-13, 19-20, 33).
writing: Definition-heavy; hedged ('We feel', 'we believe that'); new multipliers named differently from Lagrange multipliers on purpose (pp. 3, 14, 16).
limits_future: Ideal working set expensive and may not exist; nonlinear levelling only approximate; numbers deferred to [10] (pp. 21, 25, 32).

title: An introduction to the structure of large scale nonlinear optimization problems and the LANCELOT project
contribution: Tutorial on (group) partial separability via invariant subspaces and internal variables, plus the design statement of the LANCELOT project (structure, theory-code agreement plus testing, scope, SDIF input, modularity, portability).
problem_entry: Counters the view that nonlinear problems with more than 20 variables are risky to model; the view was justified ten years earlier but no longer (p. 2).
key_idea: Describe structure by element functions with large invariant subspaces and small internal variables (sparsity follows from structure, not the reverse); group them for least squares and Lagrangians; build LANCELOT around it (pp. 4-8, 11-13).
assumptions: C^2 element and group functions; smooth problems only (pp. 7, 12).
proof_devices: Theorem 1 (sparse Hessian implies partial separability), cited to Griewank-Toint (p. 7)
storage count O[3(m+1)^2] vs O[5(m+1)^2] on the minimum-surface problem (pp. 4-5)
experiments: none; pilot LANCELOT solved SDIF-specified practitioner problems with more than 1000 variables in under an hour (p. 12); detailed experiments promised (p. 13)
positioning: Builds on Griewank-Toint partial separability; discusses McCormick factorable functions, AD (Griewank), higher derivatives (Schnabel), More's problem collection; cites the CGT 1988 paper together with its correction (pp. 3, 8, 10, 13).
writing: Declared 'personnal (and maybe biased)' viewpoint; worked example before definition; LANCELOT acronym banner; numbered design requirements each with an admitted cost (pp. 3-13).
limits_future: No numbers yet; inefficiency on unstructured problems accepted; nonsmooth problems not planned; development ongoing (pp. 11-13).

title: Correction to the paper on global convergence of a class of trust region algorithms for optimization with simple bounds
contribution: Repairs the proof of Theorem 14 (finite identification of the active set) of CGT 1988 SINUM, keeping the statement and assumptions.
problem_entry: An inference in the original proof used {169}, valid only for successful iterates, for all k (p. 1).
key_idea: Restrict to successful iterates in a neighbourhood isolating a connected set of limit points, show they are all successful iterates, force Delta_k -> 0, then show all iterations are eventually successful, a contradiction (pp. 1-4).
assumptions: (AS.1)-(AS.7) and {155} of the original paper, not restated (p. 1).
proof_devices: successful-iterate subsequence inside N(X_*,delta) around an isolated connected set of limit points (eq. 6, pp. 1-2)
trapping: steps too short to leave the neighbourhood, so the subsequence equals all successful iterations (eq. 13, p. 2)
pair argument: unsuccessful k followed by successful k+1 yields rho_k >= eta, contradiction (eqs. 16-35, pp. 3-4)
decomposition of gradient and step difference into C(x_*) and its complement with a sign argument (eqs. 25-29, pp. 3-4)
positioning: Explicitly limited to correcting one error in [1]; notation and equation numbers borrowed (p. 1).
writing: Minimal-scope correction: equations of the original in braces, new proof only; credits Moré and Toraldo as finders (pp. 1, 4).
limits_future: Depends entirely on the original paper; no new results (p. 1).
